patients.summary: Retired construction worker with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and decades of heavy drinking who joined in 2020. A confusing lisinopril renewal in 2021 leads to a noncompliance label, and Dupuytren contracture appears in the right hand in 2022 and the left in 2024; last seen April 2025.

documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Mr. Sawyer phoned about moving his primary care here; previous office is in another town and he wants someone closer to Chesterfield. Medicare, no secondary. Reviewed membership terms, he is fine with them. Takes three daily pills for sugar, pressure and cholesterol. First appointment set for Mon 8/24 at 9:00, asked him to come fasting and bring all bottles. Release of records signed by email and sent to the prior primary office today.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
66 y/o man transferring care from a primary office about forty minutes away. Retired from construction (framing, then site work) a few years ago, mostly home now.

Carries type 2 diabetes, hypertension and high cholesterol, all managed by the previous office for years; he could not say when the sugar was first found. Brought his bottles: metformin 1000 mg twice a day, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Says he rarely misses. No home glucose meter in use. No chest pain, shortness of breath, leg pain on walking, foot sores or vision change.

Alcohol: he is straightforward about it. Drinks every day and has for decades, usually six to eight beers or mixed drinks across the afternoon and evening. Does not think it causes him trouble, never had withdrawal he can name, no DUIs. Never smoked. No other substances.

PSH: none. Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family: father had type 2 diabetes, mother had high blood pressure, paternal grandfather had a heart attack at 72.

Exam: well appearing, talkative. BP at goal today, see vitals. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, no thyromegaly. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly, nontender. Extremities warm, no edema. Feet: skin intact, no calluses or ulcers, monofilament sensation intact both feet, DP and PT pulses 2+. Hands unremarkable.

A/P
1. Type 2 diabetes, on metformin alone. A1c, CMP and urine albumin/creatinine today. Will get prior office records including last eye exam.
2. Hypertension, controlled on lisinopril 10.
3. Hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 40. Lipids today.
4. Alcohol use disorder, long standing, heavy daily use. AUDIT-C 12. Talked plainly about what that amount does to sugar, pressure, liver and falls. Offered naltrexone and a referral to an outpatient counselor; he would rather not right now, says he'll think about cutting back on weekdays. Door left open.
5. Health maintenance: hep C and HIV screening today (one-time). Flu shot in October. Colonoscopy history pending prior records.

Follow up 3 to 4 months, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Your Lab Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Mr. Sawyer, your labs from Monday are back. A1c is 7.2, which is close to where we want it for you. Kidney and liver tests are normal, blood counts normal, no protein in the urine. Cholesterol numbers are reasonable on the atorvastatin. Hepatitis C and HIV screens were negative. No changes for now. See you in the winter.

- Colonoscopy 2017: normal, no polyps, ten-year interval recommended.
- Pneumococcal conjugate (PCV13) given May 2019.
- Optometry diabetic eye exam June 2019: no diabetic retinopathy..
Filed to media. PCP notified.

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Here for his regular check. Nothing new; feels the same as always. Says he has not missed his metformin, lisinopril or atorvastatin. He read something online about heart attacks in diabetics and wants to know if there is anything more he should be doing to protect his heart, given his grandfather's MI.

O: BP 132/78. Remainder of vitals in flowsheet. Comfortable. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. No edema. Feet without lesions.
Fasting labs drawn this morning: A1c 6.8%, fasting glucose 138. Total cholesterol 190, LDL 90, HDL 55, triglycerides 150.

A/P
1. Cardiovascular risk: went through his picture with him. Pressure is where we want it, LDL is 90 on atorvastatin, sugar is in range. The thing most within his reach is the alcohol; six to eight drinks a day pushes up pressure and triglycerides and adds calories. Also talked about a walk most days and less takeout. He wanted a pill answer and was a little disappointed, but agreed to try cutting back. No medication changes today.
2. T2DM: A1c 6.8, continue metformin 1000 BID.
3. HTN: controlled, lisinopril 10 daily.
4. HLD: atorvastatin 40 daily.
5. AUD: as above. Still declines naltrexone or counseling.
RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: 67 y/o here for his three-month check. Tells me he is taking everything. Then, when we got to the pressure pill, he admitted he is mixed up: last week someone other than me sent a new blood pressure prescription to his new pharmacy, the label just says take as directed, and the tablets look nothing like his old ones. He can't remember what he was told about how often. He thinks some days he took one of each bottle and other days neither. Denies chest pain, palpitations or lightheadedness.

O: BP 158/92, rechecked similar. Other vitals normal. Exam unremarkable: heart regular, lungs clear, no edema.
Labs this morning: A1c 7.2%. Creatinine 1.1. TC 190, LDL 100, HDL 40, TG 250.

A/P
1. Medication noncompliance: not intentional, a labeling and bottle mix-up. The new bottle is the same drug and dose he has always taken, lisinopril 10 mg. Order rewritten with a plain once-a-morning sig and the old bottle is to come off the counter. Wrote out his three medicines on a card. Weekly pill organizer suggested and he'll buy one.
2. HTN: today's number goes with the missed and doubled doses. No change in dose. Nurse BP check in 4 weeks.
3. T2DM: A1c up a little from 6.8; HDL down and triglycerides up since June. Likely the irregular month and the drinking. Continue metformin.
4. HLD: continue atorvastatin 40.
5. AUD: no change in intake. Counseled.
6. High-dose flu vaccine today.
RTC 3 months.

Exam: BP and weight in flowsheet. Alert, oriented. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, liver not enlarged. Skin unremarkable. Feet: monofilament intact, pulses palpable. Gait steady.

Screening: colonoscopy 2017 normal, next 2027. Hep C and HIV done 2020. Pneumococcal series complete. Shingrix complete. Flu and COVID in the fall.

Alcohol: still 6 to 8 a day. Asked again about naltrexone, explained it can blunt the urge and is taken once a day; he says not yet. Offered a counseling referral, also not yet.

Plan: fasting labs drawn. Eye exam with his optometrist this summer, send the report. Return in about 5 months for diabetes.

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Diabetes check, plus a new complaint.
Right hand: for a few years has been getting stiffer, and now some fingers will not straighten all the way. Hard to grip a hammer or get his hand into a glove. No injury he remembers. No pain to speak of, no numbness.
Otherwise steady. Taking his meds from the organizer. Drinking unchanged.

Exam: vitals in flowsheet. Heart and lungs normal. Right hand: firm thickening across the palm, fingers lack full extension. Grip reasonable. Sensation intact in all fingertips, radial pulse normal.

A1c 7.2.

A/P
1. Right hand: looks like a palmar fascia problem rather than a tendon or nerve issue. Orthopedics referral placed.
2. T2DM: A1c 7.2, continue metformin.
3. HTN, HLD: continue.
4. AUD: counseled briefly.
RTC 4 months.

documents.title: Orthopedics Consultation
documents.author: orthopedics
documents.body:
Outside orthopedics consultation. Date of service: 12/23/2022. Sent on request.

Reason for referral: right hand stiffness.

HPI: 68-year-old man, retired from construction, referred by his primary physician. He was seen there for diabetes care and for a period of mixed-up blood pressure dosing. Over several years the right hand has grown steadily stiffer and some fingers no longer straighten, so gripping tools and everyday jobs have become harder. Describes the hand as tight. Once a finger curls down it stays down; no catching or popping, and the stiffness does not come and go. No injury, redness or acute pain. No numbness or tingling.

PMH: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, long-standing heavy alcohol use.
Medications: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: retired, mostly at home. Never smoker.
Family: father diabetes, mother hypertension, paternal grandfather MI at 72.

Exam, right hand: palpable longitudinal cords in the palm; fingers cannot be brought fully straight. No triggering. No skin breakdown. Sensation intact to light touch in all digits. Radial pulse palpable, capillary refill brisk.

Assessment: Dupuytren contracture, right hand.

Plan: discussed the nature of the condition, that it tends to progress slowly and is linked with diabetes and alcohol. No intervention now. He can check at home by trying to lay the hand flat on a table; if it no longer lies flat or function worsens, referral to hand surgery for treatment options. Follow up as needed.

Copy to primary care physician.

documents.title: Outside Letter Reviewed

documents.title: Hand Surgery Consultation
documents.author: hand surgery
documents.body:
Outside hand surgery consultation. Visit date: 12/11/2024. Released on request of the patient's primary physician.

Referral reason: left hand contracture.

History: 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, retired from construction. Over the past several years the left hand has stiffened and several fingers no longer extend fully, now getting in the way of daily tasks. He compares it to the right hand, which orthopedics diagnosed as Dupuytren disease in December 2022. No trauma, no infection, no numbness or tingling.

Medications: metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father diabetes, mother hypertension, paternal grandfather MI at 72.
Social: retired. Daily heavy alcohol use for many years, which is his strongest risk factor for this disease. Never smoker.

Exam: left palm with palpable longitudinal cords and incomplete active and passive extension of several fingers; right palm with established cords. Skin intact. Sensation intact to light touch throughout both hands. Radial pulses palpable, brisk capillary refill.

Impression: Dupuytren contracture, bilateral, left newly symptomatic.

Plan: reviewed percutaneous needle aponeurotomy, collagenase injection and open fasciectomy, with recurrence and recovery for each. He prefers to wait. Return when function worsens or for a decision on treatment. Encouraged to cut down on alcohol.

documents.title: Hand Surgery Follow-up
documents.author: hand surgery
documents.body:
Outside hand surgery follow-up. Visit date: 12/22/2025.

History: 71-year-old man returning for the right hand. Dupuytren disease of the right hand was first diagnosed by orthopedics in 2022 and the left hand was evaluated here in 2024. Over the past several years the right hand has grown stiffer and some fingers will not straighten; this now interferes with daily activities such as holding a cup and gripping tools. No recent injury, redness or acute pain.

Medications: metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: long history of heavy alcohol use; retired from construction.

Exam: right palm with a firm palpable cord and loss of full finger extension; tabletop test positive. Left palm cords unchanged. Sensation intact, radial pulses palpable both sides.

Assessment: progressive Dupuytren contracture, right hand, now functionally limiting.

Plan: options reviewed again. He chose percutaneous needle aponeurotomy of the right palmar cord, scheduled in clinic for January. Left hand to be revisited later.

documents.title: Needle Aponeurotomy, Right Palm
documents.author: hand surgery
documents.body:
Outside office procedure. Date: 01/26/2026.

Procedure: percutaneous needle aponeurotomy, right palmar cord.
Indication: Dupuytren contracture, right hand, limiting function.
Anesthesia: local infiltration.
Allergies: NKDA.

After consent and sterile prep, the cord was divided at several palmar portals with a small-gauge needle, followed by gentle manipulation into extension. Finger extension markedly improved on the table. Skin intact without tears. Sensation and capillary refill intact at the end. Small dressings applied.

Complications: none.
Plan: night extension splint for several months, home stretching, follow-up in hand clinic in 6 weeks.

documents.title: Outside Notes Filed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hand surgery notes from 12/22/2025 and 1/26/2026 received and read: needle release of the right palm, went well. He is still overdue to be seen here; front desk to reach out.
